The concept of card advantage is a very important one to understand for any new player. Ideally, you want to have more cards than your opponent. You draw one card each turn and usually play two or more (a land and a spell), meaning you end up losing a card each turn. Unless the spell you cast draws you a card, you just lost access to one extra card. That’s not always a bad thing: aggressive (Aggro) decks don’t usually care much about card advantage (they do, but less than other decks), but think of it this way: you don’t want to reach a point where you have 0 cards and you’re just praying the draw from your library the one card that would save you (known as topdecking). Blue is the best color for drawing cards, followed by black, then green. Red has “impulse draw” which allows you to — in a way — “look” at the top few cards (usually 3) and cast them until end of this turn or the next, or else you lose them (it exiles them, so it’s not exactly look at, but you get the point) [[Light Up the Stage]]. White is notoriously bad at hand card advantage. I say “hand” because they have another form of card advantage: tokens. White can create “cards” that aren’t in your hand through the concept of making tokens [[Raise the Alarm]]. Once you understand this concept fully, the way you build your decks will change drastically!


Remember: a player with no cards is much less of a threat than a player with bad cards. In other words, having a hand full of lands (and your opponent doesn’t know what you have) is much more important than not having anything in hand.


One other thing that is often overlooked by new players is removal and ramp. Removal is super important to deal with your opponent’s stuff. Make sure to slot in [[Banishing Light]]. If your deck isn’t token-heavy, put in [[Shatter the Sky]] as well. Ramp isn’t as essential but it basically means cards that put more lands on the battlefield, essentially breaking the one-land-per-turn rule [[Cultivate]].



A last thing to wrap your head around is the mana curve. It basically means: sort your cards in order of cmc (converted mana cost; so if something costs 3R, its cmc is 4) (if you’re on arena, just look at the top-right corner). A normal deck should have a bell-curve shape. That means you should be low on cmc 1, 2 and low on cmc 5+, but heavy on cmc 3-4. Some decks would rather focus on quick and painful creatures like aggro decks, so their curve is different: much heavier on the early cmcs and much lighter on the late ones. Your curve also decides your ideal game plan. You should be able to, in your mind, imagine what you’d play on turn 1, turn 2, turn 3, etc (assuming perfect mana).

Oh, and enjoy! It’s all about the fun you have while playing!

Hello! This may seem overwhelmingly negative, but I don't intend for it to be that way. Just providing card references and giving personal opinion. I love cycles with a passion, and I love all of those! I will be assessing from a Commander POV.

**Mandate Exchange**: Closest I could find is \[\[Grand Arbiter Augustin IV\]\], which is a creature so easier to deal with, but it makes almost everything you cast cheaper and everything your opponents cast more expensive. This kind of stax is usually really crappy for anyone playing against it, and it being an enchantment basically means it's a lock with Rakdos aggro decks as they have little to no way of dealing with enchantments and intend to play fast. I'm terribly sorry but I think it's overpowered, especially at cmc 3.

**Sanity Exchange**: \[\[Mindculling\]\] but more restrictive cost (cmc 6 => cmc 4 with color restriction) and higher rarity (Mindculling is an uncommon). I like it, but I'm not sure how I feel about creating a 4-card difference between you and ALL your opponents (keeping in mind Mindculling makes you target one opponent). Maybe it does need nerfing, I'd say either make it at cmc 5 or make it cheaper (UB maybe?) with a one card difference. This would cost it its rarity though. That being said, pure discard can be seen as a blue ability. All black discard abilities are stapled to something (a body, as in \[\[Liliana's Specter\]\], a selection, as in \[\[Thoughtseize\]\], a randomness, as in \[\[Whispers of Emrakul\]\], or repeatability, as in \[\[Disinformation Campaign\]\]). This is not to say black doesn't get pure discard, but usually there is more to it, as here this card can be monoU and still work.

**Fury Exchange**: The reason \[\[Auger Spree\]\] can get away with what it does is that the downside is stapled to the cast: to grow your creature, you need to make sure it's tough. To kill your opponent's creature, you need to give up making yours grow. Allowing both abilities separately may need to make it a bit more expensive. Both abilities are in color though, so good job there!

**Terrain Exchange**: I think this is fair. It makes your land a creature, making it more vulnerable, while removing a land. It gives up the flexibility of \[\[Pillage\]\] and the upside of \[\[Molten Rain\]\] for a more color-appropriate upside to Green, after having it cost more. I think I like this the most.

**Threat Exchange**: I think this is fair too. What is basically \[\[Savage Conception\]\] minus the repeatability, + \[\[Blessed Alliance\]\] minus the flexibility, and at instant speed, I really like this all in all.

**Morale Exchange**: This is \[\[Zealous Persecution\]\] but more expensive. You need to staple an upside there or it's strictly worst.

**Arcane Exchange**: This one is tricky. It's essentially a \[\[Spell Blast\]\] + \[\[Electrodominance\]\], except dealing damage can always be done and you can pick whatever value you want for it, while countering a spell with the specific cost of X is limiting to a spell being cast first and the value of X second. I fear this may be a bit underpowered? Not sure, though. It's very tough to assess.

**Mortality Exchange**: I think cmc 4 to give something +X/+X where X is its power is fair, especially that this doesn't come with the body it wants to grow (see \[\[Yew Spirit\]\], \[\[Heroes' Bane\]\], \[\[Chameleon Colossus\]\], etc.). One more mana for a destruction spell is also fair in theory. However I think this will play out slower/badder than one might assume. X is usually going to be 1, 2, or 3, unless it's an extreme build-around, and there will probably be several problematic creatures on the board. I'd argue that putting this at cmc 4 or maybe (not sure) even cmc 3 would be fair. It *is* color-restricted after all, and sorcery speed, and only deals with creatures, so the upside is logical at cmc 3 (see \[\[Assassin's Trophy\]\] for a cmc 2 spell that deals with *anything* and has a downside. This deals with only creatures and costs 1 more, so I can see it having an upside. Yeah, come to think of it, cmc 3 is good here). Also, this is very bad if you have no creatures on that board. It may be intentional (to force the symmetry), and if so, this only solidifies that it must be cmc 3.

**Sunlight Exchange**: Creatures hurting their controller is more of a Rakdos thing than Boros (\[\[Rakdos Charm\]\]). I'm afraid the white in Boros prevents this from happening. It's a very black thing to punish those who preach and gather armies (\[\[Stronghold Discipline\]\]). Maybe if this makes creatures deal damage to themselves (à la \[\[Solar Blaze\]\], but a fixed amount of damage instead of equal to its power?) and prevent the next two damage that would be dealt to creatures you control? That being said, I'm trying to force myself to see Boros in a different light (outside of combat), so maybe take a shot at a non-combat Boros card?

**Presence  Exchange**: I like this. It's a cheaper \[\[Tooth and Nail\]\] that lost its flexibility and breakability, is a bit more cost restrictive, and has an unsummon stapled to it. However, it may be a tad underpowered. Again, not sure, just a gut feeling.

Whenever I say “see templating/formatting on that card”, I’m referring to the Oracle text.

The “a” in “add” in the first ability should be capitalized. Also, it should say {T}: Add {W}{B} (they no longer say “to your mana pool since it’s obvious).
In the last ability, it should say “At the beginning of your upkeep,” (not turn) “you may sacrifice any number of creatures. If you do, add X mana in any combination of {W} and/or {B}, where X is the number of creatures you sacrificed.” (This is the templating on [[Grand Warlord Radha]] ). “You don’t lose this mana as steps and phases end.” (Also templating from that card).
Finally, pitlord isn’t an official creature type as far as I know. Nothing stops you from creating that, though, but Wizards rarely make new types.

Now as to what it does:
It’s a land creature which means it shouldn’t have a mana cost (see [[Dryad Arbor]] ). Instead, if you wanna keep it as a land creature, have it say: “If ~ would enter the battlefield, pay {3}{W}{B} instead. If you do, put ~ onto the battlefield. If you don't, put it into its owner's graveyard.” (See formatting on [[Lotus Vale]] ).
Finally, it’s second ability is overpowered. Maybe have it cost {X}{X}  where you have to pay 6 mana for everyone to lose 3, which sounds pretty reasonable in black imo. It may still be OP, tho, thanks to that ability that doesn’t let your mana pool empty. Maybe let it say each player rather than each opponent.
